title: Foxfield Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Foxfield wells have a 320 ft median depth, with finished-well costs modeled at $22,000-$34,400.
h1: Foxfield, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land in Foxfield means looking closely at the well record before relying on a seller’s description. Records within 5 miles show a median well depth of 320 feet, a median reported yield of 14.0 gallons per minute, and a median static water level of 161 feet below ground.

Those figures describe a large local record set, not a guarantee for one lot. A neighboring well can still differ because of aquifer position, construction, pump settings, and the exact location. The records include wells around Dove Valley, Grand View Estates, Stonegate, Centennial, Inverness, and Sierra Ridge, giving useful local context for a Foxfield purchase.

sections.heading: Foxfield well depth reflects the Denver Basin
sections.html:
Foxfield wells are commonly drilled into Denver Basin sedimentary formations, including Lower Dawson and Denver aquifers. The recorded median depth is 320 feet, while the middle half runs from 162 to 478 feet. That spread matters when you request a drilling bid: a lot near the local median should not be priced like a shallow well, and a site toward the deeper end may require substantially more drilling.

The depth mix shows 21% of wells under 100 feet, 24% from 100 to 300 feet, 42% from 300 to 600 feet, and 13% at 600 feet or deeper. The deepest recorded well is 2,510 feet. Have a driller review nearby completions rather than using the median alone.

sections.heading: Most Foxfield wells report usable production
sections.html:
Among the wells with pump-yield records, the median reported yield is 14.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half is 12.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. The records show 56% producing between 5 and 15 gallons per minute and 43% producing more than 15 gallons per minute. No recorded wells fall under 1 gallon per minute or between 1 and 5 gallons per minute in this dataset.

That is a favorable production picture for ordinary household use, but a yield test is still important. Reported pump yield can reflect different testing methods and does not by itself establish water quality, storage, pressure, or legal use. Confirm the permit’s allowed use before planning irrigation or additional buildings.

sections.heading: Water levels vary, and the decade record is uneven
sections.html:
The current record shows a median static water level of 161 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 71 to 339 feet. A pump must be selected for the actual water level and well construction, not simply for the reported well depth.

Measurements by decade are not a clean decline pattern. The median was 114 feet in the 1970s, 317 feet in the 1980s, and 538 feet in the 2000s, then 160 feet in the 2010s and 161 feet in the 2020s. Because only 166 wells report a static water level, and measurement dates and locations vary, this series does not prove that the Foxfield water table is steadily dropping. Get a current measurement for the specific well.

sections.heading: Foxfield permit history shows long local drilling activity
sections.html:
Colorado DWR records contain 5,513 permitted wells within the study area, with 2,870 recorded as constructed. Permits were issued across several decades: 1,012 in the 1970s, 962 in the 1980s, 904 in the 1990s, and 697 in the 2000s. The record also includes permits through 2025.

The most active named driller records are Hier Drilling Co Inc, associated with Bruce A. Hier, with 750 records; Authorized, associated with Pe and Pg, with 550; and Hier Drilling Co., associated with Peter J. Hier, with 528. These entries are historical permit records, not endorsements or proof of current availability. Ask for a current license, insurance, references, and a written scope.

sections.heading: A median-depth Foxfield well can be a major project
sections.html:
The local cost model uses a drilling rate of $50 to $70 per foot in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 320-foot median depth, the drilled hole is modeled at about $16,000 to $22,400. A finished well, including the pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work, is modeled at about $22,000 to $34,400.

Use those figures as a planning range, not a fixed bid. The final price can change with access, casing and grout requirements, power distance, pump selection, water testing, difficult drilling, and the actual depth needed. Get the driller to separate drilling, casing, development, pump equipment, electrical, trenching, and testing so competing bids cover the same work.

sections.heading: Foxfield buyers should check quality, yield, and site layout
sections.html:
Environmental review deserves attention before closing. Mapping within about 10 miles shows 141 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 15 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites, and 4 historic mine features. A mapped site does not establish contamination at a particular parcel, but it is a reason to order a current laboratory water test and review the site history with a qualified professional.

Low yield and dry holes remain property-specific risks even with strong area statistics. Check the well permit, construction report, pump test, static level, and water-quality results. Then verify septic setbacks, reserve area, driveway access, utility routing, and the proposed building envelope. A good well can still be a poor building site if septic and house placement conflict.

sections.heading: Before buying or building near Foxfield
sections.html:
Start with the neighboring wells nearest the parcel, especially in Dove Valley, Grand View Estates, Stonegate, Centennial, Inverness, and Sierra Ridge. Compare depth, aquifer name, yield, water level, permit use, and construction details. The records identify 100% of the wells as Denver Basin aquifer wells, with permits naming unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, Lower Dawson, and Denver formations.

Have a Colorado water professional verify the permit’s household-use rights and any limits on additional uses. If the property is in an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be needed for uses beyond the authorized exemption. Before construction, price the well and pump work alongside septic, access, trenching, and electrical work, and make the contract contingent on reviewing the actual permit and water test.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Foxfield, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth within 5 miles of Foxfield is 320 feet. The middle half ranges from 162 to 478 feet. About 42% of wells are between 300 and 600 feet, while 13% reach 600 feet or deeper. Nearby records are useful for planning, but the depth on a specific parcel can vary.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Foxfield?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the 320-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $16,000 to $22,400. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work is modeled at $22,000 to $34,400. Access and final depth can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Foxfield wells produce?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 14.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 12.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. The records show 56% producing from 5 to 15 gallons per minute and 43% above 15 gallons per minute. A parcel-specific test is still needed before relying on the well.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Foxfield, Colorado?
faq.a: Area records alone cannot establish that a particular well is safe to drink. Mapping shows 141 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles, along with 15 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Have the water tested by a certified laboratory, review nearby environmental history, and test again if the well, septic system, or surrounding land use changes.

faq.q: Are Foxfield wells getting deeper or losing water?
faq.a: The available decade series does not show a simple continuing decline. Median static water level was 114 feet in the 1970s, 538 feet in the 2000s, and 161 feet in the 2020s. Only 166 wells report static levels, and measurements vary by location and timing. Check the current water level for the specific well.
